chunks: When an operating system is needed. The question: When is it needed?
You need an OS when the software must do several things at once with different timing needs, or when you need services that are hard to write yourself, such as a network stack, USB, or a file system.
For a simple device with one or two jobs, a plain main loop is usually better. The choice should rest on numbers, not habit.
A cook with one dish needs no manager. A busy kitchen with many orders at once does. Someone has to decide who gets the stove, and an urgent order must not wait behind a slow one.
The OS is that manager. But a manager costs wages, which is the memory and CPU time an OS uses, so a tiny kitchen does better without one.
Task: one activity that the OS runs, with its own stack of working memory. Scheduler: the part of the OS that decides which task runs next.
Super-loop: one endless loop that calls each job in turn. It is the usual no-OS design. Preemption: pausing a running task so a more important one can run at once.
Bare-metal: ("What bare-metal programming is"): firmware running directly on the hardware with no OS.
A device has a control job that must run every 1 milliseconds, and a display update that takes 50 milliseconds.
In a super-loop, the control job must wait for the display update to finish, so it can be up to 50 milliseconds late.
With an RTOS (a small real-time OS), you give the control task a higher priority. It preempts the display task and runs almost at once.
The cost is RAM: four tasks with a 1 KB stack each use 4 KB, which matters on an 8 KB part. That is the whole idea.

"You need an OS when you have several concurrent activities with different timing, when a long task mustn't delay a short deadline, or when you use middleware like TCP/IP, USB or a file system that expects threads.
You need Linux-class OS for memory protection and big ecosystems.
Don't use one on tiny, ultra-low-power or very simple devices, where a super-loop plus interrupts is cheaper and simpler.
I'd decide with RAM, tick overhead and a schedulability check."
